newsitem.title: UK: UK budget to overhaul business tax regime - KPMG.
newsitem.headline: UK budget to overhaul business tax regime - KPMG.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government could include sweeping changes to the business tax regime in its July 2 budget, including an overhaul of corporate taxation and payment times, a leading tax firm said on Tuesday.
KPMG said Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown is likely keep consultation over any big changes to a minimum.

"The quick changes made to the Bank of England suggest the government is prone to acting rather than consulting and I think this will be the case with corporation tax," said Ian Barlow, head of tax at KPMG.
"Inland revenue staff are working flat out, which suggests the Chancellor is taking a radical look at business taxation and not just the measures set out in the manifesto."

Labour's manifesto said the centrepiece of the first budget would be a windfall tax on privatised utilities to fund a welfare-to-work programme, as well as a cut in the rate of indirect tax (VAT) paid on heating fuel.

Barlow predicted that, in keeping with the manifesto's promise to promote business investment, there would be no change to the 33 percent corporation tax rate, but he said tax breaks on dividends might be altered.
"The UK wants to keep attracting business to the UK and the worldwide trend in corporation tax is downward, so that suggests no change in the corporate tax rate," he said.

But Brown might float the idea of abolishing the UK's "imputation" system. This encourages the holding of equities by giving a tax credit of 20 percent on dividend payments, representing the tax the company has already paid on profits, and a return to the classic system that existed until 1973. Under the old regime, no allowance would be made to the shareholder for the tax already paid by the company on profits distributed, pushing the burden onto shareholders.
Barlow also suggested the government may consider a reduction in the payment time for corporation tax.

"That would be an easy hit for the government. At nine months from the end of the financial year, the time currently allowed is generous by internatonal standards. Most countries get companies to pay on account during the year."

Tax breaks on profit-related pay (PRP) are another easy target, KPMG said. "We are advising our clients to get any new schemes registered before July 2," said Leslie Ferrar, lead partner of KPMG's renumeration tax group.
The former Conservative government announced in its last budget that PRP would be scaled back in 1998 and abolished in 2000.

On personal taxation, the firm said it found it hard to believe the government would deliver hefty increases in income or indirect tax given Labour's manifesto commitments not to raise income tax and its criticism of VAT rises under the Conservatives.
But there are areas where the Chancellor could raise VAT without running into political problems.

"He may consider moves towards the European average for insurance premium tax. The UK's rates are well below the rates in many European countries and an increase in the rate to 12.5 percent could produce additional revenue of 2.0 billion pounds each year," KPMG said. That tax was increased to four percent from 2.5 percent at the last budget.

Duties on tobacco may be targeted, in keeping with the government's eagerness to reduce tobacco consumption, and higher duties on fuel could be excused on environmental grounds. KPMG's personal taxation expert John Battersby said he did not expect any major moves on income tax.
The budget could take an initial step towards introducing a 10 percent starting rate, although it was more likely that would come in future budgets.

"But I would imagine that inheritance tax will be higher than its current 40 percent after July 2 and that Labour will examine the rule whereby gifts can avoid inheritance tax if the giver lives for seven years after the gift is made."
